title: No one has seen a maternity denial yet. January is the real test.
summary: The 2027 maternity transition has been quiet so far, and that quiet is misleading. Almost every practice is still billing the global the way it always has, so the denials have not started. Here is why January is when we find out, and what that means for your cash flow.
body_markdown:
The most common question we get about the 2027 maternity change is some version of: how bad is this going to be? My honest answer is that no one knows yet, because the thing that would tell us has not happened.


So far, we are not seeing maternity denials tied to the transition. That sounds reassuring. It is not, and it is worth understanding why.


## Why it has been quiet


Maternity is billed once, at the end. A practice sees a patient for months of prenatal care, the delivery happens, and only then does the global bill go out, usually about 30 days later. That billing rhythm is a big part of why this has felt calm.


On top of that, almost every practice we have talked to is still billing exactly the way it always has. People are busy, the guidance is uneven, and most teams are understandably waiting to see what happens rather than changing their process in the dark. So the claims that would actually test the new rules have not gone out at scale yet.


Put those two things together and you get a system that looks fine right up until it does not.


## What January actually tests


The first large wave of 2027 deliveries gets billed in January and February. That is the moment payers either accept those globals the way they always have, or start applying whatever new rule they have quietly adopted. Some will pay. Some may partially pay. Some may deny. And because every payer is handling the transition differently, you may see all three at once.


Realistically, I think there is a small chance this goes smoothly, where every payer announces in time and every system updates cleanly. I think there is a larger chance it is messy for a while, with a higher volume of denials than usual, as practices and payers both work through a transition that none of them have done before.


And it lands at the worst possible time: the start of a new plan year, when deductibles reset and patients churn between plans. That new-year noise alone makes denials harder to spot and triage.


## What to do with a quiet November


The quiet is not a reason to relax. It is the window to prepare. A few things worth doing now:


- Know which payers your patients actually have, and pull each one's maternity policy rather than assuming.
- Flag the deliveries coming in January and February whose care began in 2026, because those cross-year cases are where the ambiguity lives.
- Decide, payer by payer, how you intend to bill before the claim goes out, not after it comes back denied.


We built a free[maternity resource center](https://www.substrateai.com/payers/2027-substrate-maternity-resource-center) to make that first step easier: a single place to find each payer's policy and track what has changed. The teams that come through January in good shape will be the ones that treated this quiet stretch as preparation time.
